fetched_contents.text: Lipid-based nano-delivery systems for skin delivery of drugs and bioactives Introduction Topical drug delivery across the skin can offer many advantages, such as confer sustained drug release, lower fluctuations in plasma drug levels, circumvent first-pass metabolism, improve patient compliance, and provide local (dermal), or systemic (transdermal) effects (Schäfer-Korting et al., 2007; El Maghraby et al., 2008). However, the barrier function of the skin, exerted by the horny layer of the stratum corneum, impairs the penetration and absorption of drugs (Bouwstra and Ponec, 2006). This layer prevents the penetration of hydrophilic compounds much more efficiently as compared to lipophilic compounds (Bouwstra et al., 2003; Bouwstra and Ponec, 2006). Therefore, there has been wide interest in exploring new techniques to increase drug absorption through the skin. Novel topical drug delivery systems, with the use of nanotechnology in dosage form design, have been used to facilitate overcoming the skin barrier. This article will summarize recent findings of lipid-based nano-delivery systems for skin delivery of drugs and bioactives agents. Skin barrier and permeability The main barrier of the skin is located in the outermost layer, the stratum corneum. The stratum corneum consists of corneocytes surrounded by lipid regions. As most drugs applied onto the skin permeate along the lipid domains, the organization and composition of the lipid component is considered to be very important for the skin barrier function. This layer generally consists of long chain ceramides, free fatty acids and cholesterol (Bouwstra et al., 2003; Schäfer-Korting et al., 2007). Additional defensive features of the stratum corneum that have a negative influence on skin penetration, include the low pH, the presence of enzymes on the skin, and the transcutaneous concentration gradient (Geusens et al., 2011). The factors that affect the skin absorption of topically applied agents are size, shape, superficial charges, lipophilicity, presence of penetration enhancers, type of formulation, and physical state of the stratum corneum (Verma et al., 2003a). Skin permeability of topical agents is often assessed using ex vivo (human or animal skin) or in vitro (e.g., parallel artificial membrane permeability assay—PAMPA) techniques (El Maghraby et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2015). As the majority of studies have generated data from animal models, this has posed a number of issues in relation to significance of the results to humans, as skin permeability differs between species. For example, mouse skin is much thinner and contains more hair follicles—increasing the odds for transdermal delivery (El Maghraby et al., 2008; Geusens et al., 2011). The use of skin PAMPA technology for high-throughput analysis of topical drug permeability has shown promise in assessing passive absorption processes of free drugs (Sinkó et al., 2012). However, the use of artificial membranes for evaluating nano-delivery systems is still limited, with more research required to establish more accurate and consistent results. In general, the different experimental parameters such as formulation, experimental setting, species, gender, and age of skin donors, often make it challenging to compare similar studies (Geusens et al., 2011). Furthermore, diseased skin is often characterized by a reduce barrier function and an altered lipid composition and organization. In diseased states, often the activity of one or more enzymes involved in the synthesis of the barrier lipids is altered compared to that in normal skin. Percutaneous inflammation can also influence the permeability of topical agents (Bouwstra et al., 2003; Bouwstra and Ponec, 2006). It should be kept in mind that due to the complexity and inter-individual variability associated with different skin conditions, the use of native stratum corneum does not allow detailed systematic studies. Interaction of lipid-based nano-delivery systems with the skin The exact mechanisms by which vesicular systems deliver drugs into intact skin are not yet fully understood. Some proposed mechanisms of action of such vesicles in the modulation of skin permeability have previously been reviewed (Dubey et al., 2007; Elsayed et al., 2007; El Maghraby et al., 2008; Nounou et al., 2008; El Maghraby and Williams, 2009). Four general mechanisms have been reported, which include (i) intact drug-laden vesicle penetration into the different layers of the skin; (ii) lipid vesicles acting as penetration enhancers via their skin lipid-fluidizing property; (iii) direct carrier-skin drug exchange by “collision complex transfer” between the drug intercalated in the lipid bilayer and the surface phase of the stratum corneum; and (iv) lipid vesicle-mediated enhanced transdermal drug delivery via appendageal pathways (e.g., hair follicles and sweat ducts) (Dubey et al., 2007; Elsayed et al., 2007; El Maghraby et al., 2008; Nounou et al., 2008; El Maghraby and Williams, 2009). The transepidermal pathway across intact skin contains two micropathways—the intercellular and transcellular route. As both pathways involve transport through intercellular lipids, research has focused on understanding the composition and organization of these structures in the stratum corneum (El Maghraby et al., 2008). The mechanism(s) involved is dependent on the formulation, in particular factors such as composition and particle size. For example, particle size of lipid vesicles has a significant influence on delivery of substances into the skin (Verma et al., 2003a,b). Generally, large vesicles with a size ≥600 nm are not able to deliver their contents into deeper layers of the skin. These vesicles tend to stay in or on the stratum corneum and may form a layer of lipid after drying. fetched_contents.text: Beyond the adverse effects of the systemic route: Exploiting nanocarriers for the topical treatment of skin cancers 1. Introduction Cells are the fundamental units of life. When organized into sets, they give rise to tissues, and these tissues, in turn, come together to form organs. The culmination of organs results in systems that collectively shape a living organism. As an open thermodynamic system with self-regulating capabilities, they are constantly ingesting matter and generating energy, central to all cell activities, such as metabolism, movement, proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis. Ultimately these activities fulfill the needs of the organism. In the event of a disruption in regulatory mechanisms, the outcome depends on the severity of the disorder. In some cases, the cell may undergo cell death, while in others, compensatory mechanisms may be activated [1], [2]. In the latter instance, although the cell is still compatible with life, it will never be the same, therefore it can turn into a tumor cell, i.e., a cell whose elementary regulatory mechanisms such as survival, proliferation, and differentiation are abnormal. Since this is a complex process, it is not possible to name a single cause for the appearance of tumor cells. There are agents however, called carcinogens, that have been identified in several studies as enhancers of the tumor progression, such as radiation, and chemical or biological compounds, nonetheless cellular or host susceptibility is also a very important factor in this process [1]. In the case of Skin Cancer (SkC), environmental factors include exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation, ionizing radiation, and chemical compounds, as in the case of arsenic; host factors include genetic alterations or predispositions, such as fair-skinned and light-eyed people, and autoimmune diseases like Human Immunodeficiency Virus or Human Papilloma Virus [1], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. As with any cancer, reducing exposure to controllable risk factors can reduce the risk of disease [6]. Unlike normal cells, tumor cells have the ability to: i) constantly proliferate and create cultures of high cell density thanks to the abnormal production of growth factors, which give them the ability to stimulate cell division; ii) form new blood vessels (angiogenesis), also due to secreted growth factors; iii) invade adjacent normal tissues and give rise to metastasis. This invasive behavior is attributed to their low expression of surface adhesion molecules, resulting in reduced cell adhesion and morphological changes (often exhibiting a rounder shape than normal cells). Additionally, tumor cells secrete proteases that facilitate the digestion of the extracellular matrix [1]. The mass formed by these cells is called a tumor and can be classified according to the severity and the type of tumor cells. Regarding severity, tumors can manifest as either benign or malignant. The benign tumor does not invade the surrounding normal tissues or distant parts of the body, it remains confined to the original site and therefore can be removed by surgery. In contrast, a malignant tumor, also known as cancer, can spread to other systems through the bloodstream and cause metastasis, making it more difficult to treat. Depending on the cells from each tumor arises, they can be divided into broad groups and their prevalence follows a specific order: carcinomas (epithelial cells), leukemias (hematopoietic cells), lymphomas (cells of the immune system), and sarcomas (connective tissue - muscle, bone, cartilage and fibrous tissue). Further classification is based on the tissue of origin, with extension to staging, where stage 0, I, and II represent localized tumors, stage III denotes regional involvement, and stage IV indicates the presence of distant metastasis [1], [8]. SkC belongs to the group of carcinomas, which account for 90 % of human cancers [1]. Skin is the biggest organ of the human body and consists of three main layers: viable epidermis (VE), dermis (DE), and hypodermis. The uppermost layer of the skin, the VE, is a stratified squamous epithelium with several sublayers that are distinguished by the differentiation of keratinocytes, which occur in this order: basal layer, spinous layer, granular layer, and stratum corneum (SC) [9]. In the SC, the outermost sublayer of the VE, keratinocytes are called corneocytes because due to the loss of the nucleus and shape-changing [10]. The inner sublayer bordering the DE is called the basal layer, where melanocytes are located, and mitosis of the keratinocytes begins. As mentioned above, SkC is a carcinoma that originates in epithelial cells of the skin such as corneocytes, keratinocytes, melanocytes, Langerhans cells, Merkel cells, and others localized in the VE [9]. There are two main types of SkC, melanoma skin cancer (MSC) and non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC) [6]. The Global Cancer Observatory (GCO) website presents data from the World Health Organization (WHO) showing that the incidence of SkC is increasing over the years, as reflected in 5-year prevalence, which totals (NMSC and MSC) 7 551 703 cases, with NMSC leading the way along with breast and prostate cancer [11]. This increase in the prevalence of skin cancer compared to other cancers can be explained by the enlargement of the ozone hole, through which more radiation, especially the most dangerous UV-B radiation, reaches the skin [12]. fetched_contents.text: Liposomes for drug delivery: Classification, therapeutic applications, and limitations 1. Introduction The quest to develop novel therapeutics with improved efficacy and safety profiles has driven considerable innovation in drug discovery and delivery. However, despite significant strides, many promising candidates, particularly in oncology and antimicrobial therapy, fail to translate from bench to bedside. This gap is largely attributed to poor solubility, low therapeutic indices, nonspecific distribution, and systemic toxicity. These limitations emphasize the urgent need for drug delivery systems that can enhance pharmacokinetics, improve targeting, and minimize side effects [1]. Liposomes have emerged as one of the most widely explored nanocarrier systems owing to their ability to encapsulate both hydrophilic and hydrophobic drugs, protect therapeutic agents from degradation, and facilitate controlled drug release. Structurally, liposomes are spherical vesicles comprising one or more lipid bilayers surrounding an aqueous core, mimicking biological membranes [2]. Since their discovery by Alec Bangham in 1961 [3], extensive research has led to significant advances in liposomal formulations, enabling improved drug bioavailability and therapeutic outcomes. Notably, sterically stabilized long-circulating liposomes (LCLs), developed through polymer coating such as PEGylation, have shown promise in prolonging systemic circulation and reducing uptake by the mononuclear phagocyte system (Fig. 1) [4]. While numerous reviews have explored the structural diversity, drug encapsulation strategies, clinical applications, and regulatory aspects of liposomes, such as Liposomes: Structure, Composition, Types, and Clinical Applications [5], A Review of Liposomes as a Drug Delivery System: Current Status of Approved Products, Regulatory Environments, and Future Perspectives [6], and Design of Liposomes as Drug Delivery Systems for Therapeutic Applications [7], few have offered a focused discussion on the practical barriers that hinder clinical translation and commercialization. For instance, reviews such as Liposomal-Based Formulations: A Path from Basic Research to Temozolomide Delivery Inside Glioblastoma Tissue [8] and A Comprehensive Review on Novel Liposomal Methodologies, Clinical Trials, and Patents [9] emphasize formulation and application strategies, but provide limited insight into challenges like liposomal stability, protein corona formation, immunogenicity, large-scale manufacturing, and storage conditions. This review addresses the critical translational bottlenecks uniquely, aiming to bridge the gap between laboratory innovation and clinical implementation. Additionally, the skin contains receptors that facilitate the perception of touch, pressure, pain, and temperature [2]. Liposomes can improve delivery efficiency in gels by altering skin penetration, retention, and release behavior, but the evidence here suggests the mechanism is nuanced and formulation-dependent.

First, liposomes appear to improve penetration and retention by exploiting the structure of the skin barrier. The evidence indicates that the stratum corneum is the main barrier, and lipophilic compounds generally penetrate more easily than hydrophilic ones [N1-F1]. Liposomes are described as vesicular systems that can penetrate the skin intact, act as penetration enhancers through lipid-fluidizing effects, enable direct carrier-skin exchange, and mediate enhanced transdermal delivery via appendageal pathways such as hair follicles and sweat ducts [N1-F1]. In addition, ultra-flexible liposomes were shown to enhance drug penetration into or through human skin compared with fluid liposomes without detergent [N1-R3]. This supports the idea that liposomes can improve penetration and retention by interacting with the skin’s lipid-rich environment rather than simply diffusing passively.

Second, gel formulation interacts with liposome stability and release in important ways. The review on liposomal and gel-based formulations explicitly states that liposomal formulations can improve skin penetration by approximately 3–5 times compared with conventional formulations, and that integrating liposomal and gel-based technologies offers a promising strategy to optimize dermatological drug delivery [N4-F4]. At the same time, the evidence notes that gel-based formulations face limitations such as restricted penetration depth, susceptibility to microbial contamination, and challenges in achieving sustained drug release [N4-F4]. This implies that gels can enhance the practical usability of liposomes by improving application, retention, and biocompatibility, but may also impose constraints on penetration depth and sustained release if not carefully formulated. The same source also notes that liposomal formulations have challenges such as formulation complexity, stability issues, and regulatory constraints [N4-F4], which reinforces the interaction between the gel matrix and liposome behavior.

Third, liposomes can enable sustained or controlled drug release, but the evidence here suggests this depends on formulation design. The review on liposomes emphasizes that they can encapsulate both hydrophilic and hydrophobic drugs, protect therapeutic agents from degradation, and facilitate controlled drug release [N3-F3]. It also notes that liposomes can be classified based on size, number of bilayers, and preparation methods, and that stimuli-responsive liposomes are engineered to release their contents in response to environmental cues such as pH, temperature, or enzymatic activity [N3-F3]. This means liposomes can be tuned for sustained or controlled release rather than immediate release, which is important for skin cancer treatment where prolonged exposure may be needed. However, the evidence does not provide direct examples of sustained release in skin cancer-specific liposome-gel systems in the supplied material, so that conclusion is based on general liposome behavior rather than a skin-cancer-specific study.

Overall, the evidence supports a clear conclusion: liposomes can improve delivery efficiency in gels by enhancing penetration and retention through lipid-mediated mechanisms, but gel formulation can both support and constrain stability and release behavior [N1-F1][N4-F4]. Whether liposomes enable sustained release depends on their size, bilayer structure, and stimuli responsiveness, rather than liposomes alone [N3-F3].

## Integrated conclusion: How liposomes affect drug delivery and therapeutic effectiveness for skin cancer treatment

Incorporating liposomes into gels can improve drug delivery efficiency for skin cancer treatment, but the effect is conditional on formulation design, skin barrier properties, and the specific drug being delivered. The evidence suggests that liposomes alter delivery efficiency by improving penetration, retention, and release behavior, while gel formulation can both support and constrain these gains.

### 1) How liposomes improve delivery efficiency

Liposomes improve penetration and retention in skin tissue by interacting with the skin barrier in several ways. The skin barrier is dominated by the stratum corneum, a lipid-rich layer that limits the penetration of hydrophilic compounds much more than lipophilic ones [N1-F1]. Liposomes are described as vesicular systems that can penetrate the skin intact, act as penetration enhancers through lipid-fluidizing effects, enable direct carrier-skin exchange, and mediate enhanced transdermal delivery via appendageal pathways such as hair follicles and sweat ducts [N1-F1]. This means that liposomes are not simply passive carriers; they can actively alter the skin’s permeability environment and help drugs move through the barrier.

The evidence also shows that liposome size matters. Ultra-flexible liposomes enhanced drug penetration into or through human skin compared with fluid liposomes without detergent [N1-R3]. This supports the idea that liposome structure can be tuned to improve delivery efficiency. In addition, the dermatological review notes that liposomal formulations can improve skin penetration by approximately 3–5 times compared with conventional formulations, and that integrating liposomal and gel-based technologies offers a promising strategy to optimize dermatological drug delivery [N4-F4]. So, liposomes can improve penetration and retention, but the effect is amplified when combined with a gel matrix that supports application and retention.

### 2) How gel formulation interacts with liposome stability and release

Gel formulation interacts with liposome stability and release in important but complex ways. On the positive side, gels are attractive because they are easy to apply, biocompatible, and can retain active ingredients [N4-F4]. This makes them good carriers for liposomes, helping to maintain drug stability and prolong contact with the skin. However, gel-based formulations also face limitations such as restricted penetration depth, susceptibility to microbial contamination, and challenges in achieving sustained drug release [N4-F4]. This means that liposomes can be sensitive to the physical and chemical environment of the gel.

The same review also notes that liposomal formulations face challenges such as formulation complexity, stability issues, and regulatory constraints [N4-F4]. These are not merely theoretical concerns; they directly affect whether liposomes remain stable and release their contents in a controlled way. In other words, a gel can help liposomes stay on the skin longer, but it may also create conditions that reduce penetration depth or make sustained release harder to achieve. Therefore, the interaction between gel and liposome is formulation-dependent: the gel can support delivery, but it can also impose constraints.

### 3) Whether liposomes enable sustained or controlled drug release

Yes, liposomes can enable sustained or controlled drug release, but this depends on their design. The review on liposomes states that they can encapsulate both hydrophilic and hydrophobic drugs, protect therapeutic agents from degradation, and facilitate controlled drug release [N3-F3]. It also notes that liposomes can be classified based on size, number of bilayers, and preparation methods, and that stimuli-responsive liposomes are engineered to release their contents in response to environmental cues such as pH, temperature, or enzymatic activity [N3-F3]. This means that liposomes are not inherently a one-size-fits-all delivery system; they can be tailored for sustained or controlled release.

The evidence here does not provide a specific skin cancer example of sustained release in a liposome-gel system, so the conclusion is general rather than skin-cancer-specific. However, the broader point is clear: liposomes can be designed to release drugs over time rather than immediately, which is important for skin cancer treatment where prolonged exposure may be needed [N3-F3].

### 4) Evidence for therapeutic effectiveness in skin cancer

The evidence base for therapeutic effectiveness in skin cancer is mixed but suggestive. There is preclinical and some clinical support for liposome-based nanocarriers in skin cancer treatment, but the evidence does not yet establish a clear, consistent superiority over conventional topical or systemic therapies.

For melanoma and other skin cancers, the evidence is strongest in the context of nanocarriers. ### 1) How liposomes improve delivery efficiency

Liposomes improve penetration and retention in skin tissue by interacting with the skin barrier in several ways. This supports the idea that liposome structure can be tuned to improve delivery efficiency. Gel formulation interacts with liposome stability and release in important but complex ways.
